name: Printing Consecutive Numbers Starting from Zero (Case 2)
description: Construct a program that prints a sequence of numbers from 0 (inclusive) to 6 (exclusive).
code:
#Step 1: Iterate through the numbers in the sequence
for num in range(6): 
    #Step 1.1: Print each number in the sequence
    print(num)

1.content: #Step 1: Iterate through the numbers in the sequence

commentList: Purpose: This line starts a for-loop that runs the indented block once for each number produced by range(6). You will get the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in sequence, so the print inside the loop runs six times.

Syntax breakdown: for num in range(6): — 'for' begins the loop, 'num' is the loop variable that receives each value, 'in' says you iterate over the sequence returned by range(6), and the trailing ':' marks the loop header. The code that belongs to the loop must be indented under this line.

Semantics / common source of confusion: range(6) gives values from 0 up to but not including 6. If you expected 6 to appear, that's an off-by-one mistake. To start from a different number, you would use range(start, stop).

Potential errors and misconceptions: If you forget the colon you'll get a SyntaxError; incorrect indentation of the body will cause an IndentationError or unexpected behavior. A frequent misconception is thinking range(6) returns a list — it yields values one at a time as you iterate.

Best practices: Use a clear loop variable name like 'num' for readability; if you don't use the loop variable, name it '_' to show it's unused. Avoid modifying the loop variable inside the loop. If you truly need a list of values for indexing or inspection, use list(range(6)), otherwise iterate directly over range(6).

3.content: #Step 1.1: Print each number in the sequence

commentList: You use print(num) to output the current value of num to the console so the program displays each number produced by the loop.

You are calling Python's built-in print function with num as its argument: the function converts num to text and writes it followed by a newline by default; num is the loop variable that changes each iteration.

Be careful: if you write print('num') with quotes you will print the literal word "num" instead of the variable's value; forgetting parentheses (print num) causes a SyntaxError in Python 3; misindentation can make the line run outside the loop or raise an IndentationError; a misspelled variable name will raise a NameError.

As a best practice, use print for simple output or debugging—if you want numbers on the same line use print(num, end=' ') or build a formatted string; choose clear variable names and avoid putting complex expressions with side effects directly inside print.

Step-by-step: if you use this line, the loop will start at 1 and iterate through 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. You might pick this because you believe numeric sequences naturally begin at 1 or because you think you must explicitly skip 0. The practical effect is that the value 0 will never be printed, so your output will be missing the first value of the intended sequence. Compared to the intended loop setup, this line misimplements the lower bound: it begins one step too high. That off-by-one at the start makes the program produce a sequence that is shifted up by one, which is why this choice is incorrect.

commentList: Step-by-step: with this line, the loop will iterate over 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. You may be tempted to write this because you think the upper number given to range must be increased by one to include the desired final value. The effect is that the loop prints one extra number (the value 6), which goes beyond the intended end of the sequence. In other words, this choice misimplements the upper bound by including an extra element; it causes the program to produce a longer sequence than required.
